name: Executive Order of October 3, 1873 establishing the Tule River Reservation in place of the reserve of January 9, 1873
nations: Bands Royce lists as King's River, Owen's River and Tule River Indians (Yokuts and Mono peoples)
promises: No treaty: the President cancelled the reserve made by executive order on January 9, 1873 and set apart in its place a Tule River reservation in the mountains on the South Fork of the Tule River (Royce). Royce marks area 547 as land added to the former reserve.

The Tule River Tribe's account says the 1873 reservation replaced the earlier farm land on the valley floor near Porterville and was about doubled, to 91,837 acres, later that year because the new land was unsuited to farming.

breaches.what: The Tule River Tribe says that President Hayes's executive order of 1878 cut the reservation back to about its original size and that the President lacked authority under federal law to reduce it, and that in 1876 its people on the Madden Farm were forcibly removed to the new reservation.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Tule River Indian Tribe, with the Native American Rights Fund, water settlement presentation, September 24, 2013

source.title: Tule River Indian Tribe Water Settlement (presentation by the Tule River Tribe, Tom Rodgers, the Native American Rights Fund, GEI and NRCE, September 24, 2013)
source.publisher: Native American Rights Fund, National Indian Law Library

breaches.quote: The President lacked the authority under federal law to reduced the size of the Reservation.

landTaken: Royce records that the Executive Order of August 3, 1878 restored to the public domain part of the reservation set apart on October 3, 1873, and that the remainder is the present Tule River reserve. The Tribe's 2013 presentation gives the present reservation as 55,396 acres.
today: The Tule River Reservation remains the Tribe's homeland. No court or Claims Commission finding on the 1878 reduction was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history, presented with the Native American Rights Fund, says its ancestors signed the unratified 1851 Treaty of Paint Creek, that its first reservation of valley farmland was taken by Indian agents through state patents, that its people were removed to the mountain reservation, and that the 1878 reduction was beyond the President's authority.

In 2024 House testimony, Vice Chairman Lester Shine Nieto said the 1856 reservation of about 2,440 acres of valley farmland was partly taken through fraudulent land warrants issued to Indian agents Madden and Benson, which the United States never challenged, that in 1873 the Tribe was forcibly removed to mountainous land it protested, and that the August 1878 executive order unlawfully cut the enlarged 91,837 acre reservation back to about 48,000 acres.

openQuestions: The executive orders of January 9 and October 3, 1873 were read only in Royce's summary; their acreages (48,000 and 91,837 acres) come from the Tribe's presentation, not the orders.

Decided by Jordan 2026-11-08: an executive order taking back executive-order land is not a breach by itself; it needs a finding. the 1878 reduction took back land set apart by an executive order, not by a treaty. Without a court or Commission finding it stays contested, resting on the Tribe's statement that the President lacked authority.

The Indians of California claims (ICC Dockets 31 and 37) covered aboriginal California land generally, not this executive order; they were not reviewed for this file. The 1851 Treaty of Paint Creek belongs to the unratified California treaties.
treaties.json lists Big Sandy, Cold Springs and North Fork Mono rancherias as present-day tribes; their link to this reservation was not checked. The Tribe's own website was not opened.

plain.promised: There was no treaty. In 1873 the President set apart a Tule River reservation in the mountains in place of an earlier one. The Tribe says it was about doubled that year because the land was poor for farming.
plain.happened: In 1878 a new executive order returned part of it to the public domain. The Tule River Tribe says the President had no authority to shrink it. No court or claims commission finding was found.
plain.today: The remainder is the Tule River Reservation, 55,396 acres by the Tribe's count. Nothing paid or returned for the 1878 reduction was found.
